bmt-2021-power-01a.title: Read off the edges
bmt-2021-power-01a.body: Each element $\{x,y\}$ of $E$ is an edge between $x$ and $y$. Draw the five points $a,b,c,d,e$, join consecutive points $ab,bc,cd,de,ea$ to make a $5$-cycle, and add the sixth edge $ad$ as a chord. How the picture is laid out does not matter; only the vertices and which pairs are joined.

bmt-2021-power-01b.title: List all pairs
bmt-2021-power-01b.body: Take $V_5=\{a,b,c,d,e\}$. Every pair of distinct vertices is an edge, so $E_5=\{\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{a,d\},\{a,e\},\{b,c\},\{b,d\},\{b,e\},\{c,d\},\{c,e\},\{d,e\}\}$.

bmt-2021-power-01c.title: Count pairs
bmt-2021-power-01c.body:
Every pair of the $5$ vertices is joined by exactly one edge, so the number of edges is $\binom52=10$. (The drawing is a pentagon with all five diagonals.)

**Answer: 10**

bmt-2021-power-01d.title: Choose two vertices
bmt-2021-power-01d.body:
An edge corresponds to a choice of $2$ distinct vertices out of $n$, so there are $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$ edges.

**Answer: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$**

bmt-2021-power-02.title: Shapes times labelings
bmt-2021-power-02.body:
There are $5$ possible shapes with $3$ nodes (the Catalan number $C_3=\frac14\binom63=5$): the possible ways to place the three nodes in a binary tree. Each shape can be labeled in $3!=6$ ways, giving $5\cdot6=30$.

(Shapes: all three nodes in a chain, with each step going left or right: $4$ shapes; plus the shape with a root having two node children: $1$ shape; total $5$.)

**Answer: 30**

bmt-2021-power-03.title: Induction on $n$
bmt-2021-power-03.body:
**Claim: a tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges.**

For $n=1$ the tree has no edges. Suppose every tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges and let $T$ be a tree on $n+1\ge2$ vertices.

*$T$ has a vertex of degree $1$.* Take a longest path $v_0v_1\cdots v_k$ in $T$ ($k\ge1$ since $T$ is connected with at least $2$ vertices). If $v_0$ had another neighbor $w\ne v_1$, then either $w$ is on the path (giving a cycle, contradicting the uniqueness of paths) or $w$ extends the path (contradicting maximality). So $v_0$ has degree $1$.

Removing $v_0$ and its edge leaves a connected graph in which paths are still unique, so a tree on $n$ vertices, with $n-1$ edges by the induction hypothesis. Hence $T$ has $(n-1)+1=n$ edges. ∎

bmt-2021-power-04c.title: Identity
bmt-2021-power-04c.body:
$\sigma$ is the identity permutation, so every power is the identity: $\sigma^3=(12345)'$.

**Answer: $(12345)'$**

bmt-2021-power-05a.title: Inclusion-exclusion
bmt-2021-power-05a.body:
Let $A_i$ be the set of permutations fixing $i$. By inclusion-exclusion, the number with at least one fixed point is $\binom41\cdot3!-\binom42\cdot2!+\binom43\cdot1!-\binom44\cdot0!=24-12+4-1=15$. So the number of permutations with no fixed point is $24-15=9$.

**Answer: 9**

bmt-2021-power-05b.title: Choose the fixed point
bmt-2021-power-05b.body:
Choose the fixed element in $5$ ways; the other four elements must form a permutation of those four with no fixed point, and there are $9$ of these (derangements of $[4]$). Total $5\cdot9=45$.

**Answer: 45**

bmt-2021-power-05c.title: The two moved elements swap
bmt-2021-power-05c.body:
If exactly two elements $i\ne j$ are not fixed, then $\sigma$ maps $\{i,j\}$ onto itself (everything else is fixed) without fixing either, so $\sigma(i)=j$ and $\sigma(j)=i$. Thus each choice of the pair $\{i,j\}$ gives exactly one such permutation, and there are $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ of them.

**Answer: $\frac{n(n-1)}2$**

bmt-2021-power-06.title: Each other number goes left or right of the peak
bmt-2021-power-06.body:
The peak must be the value $n$. Each of the other $n-1$ numbers is placed either to the left of $n$ (these appear in increasing order) or to its right (in decreasing order), and each such choice gives exactly one arrangement. This gives $2^{n-1}$ arrangements. The peak is at an end (not allowed) exactly when all numbers go to the right (the decreasing permutation) or all go to the left (the increasing one): $2$ arrangements. So there are $2^{n-1}-2$.

**Answer: $2^{n-1}-2$**

bmt-2021-power-07.title: Count by cycle type
bmt-2021-power-07.body:
An involution consists only of fixed points and swaps. For $[4]$: the identity ($1$); one swap and two fixed points ($\binom42=6$); two swaps ($3$: $(2143)'$, $(3412)'$, $(4321)'$). Total $1+6+3=10$.

**Answer: 10**

bmt-2021-power-08.title: Strong induction with pigeonhole
bmt-2021-power-08.body:
We use strong induction on $n$. For $n=1$, $\sigma=(1)$.

Let $n\ge2$ and $\sigma$ a permutation of $[n]$. Take any $x\in[n]$ and consider $x,\sigma(x),\sigma^2(x),\dots$. They all lie in the finite set $[n]$, so by pigeonhole two coincide: $\sigma^i(x)=\sigma^j(x)$ with $i<j$. Since $\sigma$ is a bijection we can apply $\sigma^{-i}$ to get $\sigma^{j-i}(x)=x$. Let $k\ge1$ be the smallest positive integer with $\sigma^k(x)=x$. The elements $x,\sigma(x),\dots,\sigma^{k-1}(x)$ are distinct (if $\sigma^i(x)=\sigma^j(x)$ with $0\le i<j<k$ then $\sigma^{j-i}(x)=x$, contradicting minimality), and they form the cycle $C=(x\ \sigma(x)\ \cdots\ \sigma^{k-1}(x))$.

If $C$ contains all of $[n]$, we are done. Otherwise $\sigma$ maps $T=[n]\setminus C$ into itself (as $\sigma$ permutes $C$ among itself and is a bijection), so $\sigma|_T$ is a permutation of a set with fewer than $n$ elements, which by the induction hypothesis is a product of disjoint cycles. Together with $C$ this writes $\sigma$ in cycle notation. ∎

bmt-2021-power-10a.title: Parity
bmt-2021-power-10a.body:
A sum of even numbers is even, so $7$ has no such partition: $p_e(7)=0$.

**Answer: 0**

bmt-2021-power-10c.title: List
bmt-2021-power-10c.body:
The partitions of $7$ into distinct parts: $7$, $6+1$, $5+2$, $4+3$, $4+2+1$. So $p_d(7)=5$.

**Answer: 5**

bmt-2021-power-11.title: A bijection
bmt-2021-power-11.body:
**Odd $\to$ distinct.** Take a partition of $n$ into odd parts, in which the odd number $i$ appears $m_i$ times, so $n=\sum_i m_i\,i$. Write each multiplicity in binary, $m_i=2^{x_1}+2^{x_2}+\cdots$ (distinct powers of two), and replace the $m_i$ copies of $i$ by the parts $i\cdot2^{x_1},\,i\cdot2^{x_2},\dots$. The sum is unchanged. The new parts are distinct: each is of the form (odd)$\cdot2^b$, and this representation of an integer is unique, so two new parts coincide only if they come from the same $i$ and the same power of two, which does not happen.

**Distinct $\to$ odd.** Take a partition into distinct parts $d_1,\dots,d_k$ and write each uniquely as $d_j=c_j2^{b_j}$ with $c_j$ odd. Replace $d_j$ by $2^{b_j}$ copies of the odd part $c_j$. The sum is unchanged and all parts are odd.

These two maps are inverse to each other: in the distinct$\to$odd direction the multiplicity of $c$ is $\sum2^{b_j}$ over the parts $c\cdot2^{b_j}$, which is the binary expansion with distinct powers (the $d_j$ are distinct, so the $b_j$ for fixed $c$ are distinct), and the odd$\to$distinct map recovers exactly those parts. Hence the two sets are in bijection and $p_d(n)=p_o(n)$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-12.title: Whether 1 is a part
bmt-2021-power-12.body:
Partitions of $n$ into $k$ parts are of two kinds.

- Those containing a part equal to $1$: removing one $1$ gives a partition of $n-1$ into $k-1$ parts, and this is reversible (add a part $1$). There are $p(n-1,k-1)$ of these.
- Those with all parts $\ge2$: subtracting $1$ from every part gives a partition of $n-k$ into $k$ parts (positive parts), and this is reversible (add $1$ to every part). There are $p(n-k,k)$ of these.

Adding the two counts gives $p(n,k)=p(n-1,k-1)+p(n-k,k)$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-13.title: Condition on the block containing 4
bmt-2021-power-13.body:
Remove the block $S$ containing $4$. If the remaining $k$ elements (chosen from $\{1,2,3\}$ in $\binom3k$ ways) are partitioned in $\mathrm{Par}(k)$ ways, we get $\mathrm{Par}(4)=\binom30\cdot1+\binom31\cdot1+\binom32\cdot2+\binom33\cdot5=1+3+6+5=15$.

**Answer: 15**

bmt-2021-power-15.title: Multiply out
bmt-2021-power-15.body: $A(z)B(z)=\sum_{m,j\ge0}\frac{a_mb_j}{m!\,j!}z^{m+j}=\sum_{m,j}\binom{m+j}{m}a_mb_j\frac{z^{m+j}}{(m+j)!}$. Collecting terms with $m+j=n$: $A(z)B(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}\left(\sum_{m=0}^n\binom nma_mb_{n-m}\right)\frac{z^n}{n!}$. Comparing coefficients of $\frac{z^n}{n!}$ gives the formula. ∎

bmt-2021-power-16.title: Compare coefficients
bmt-2021-power-16.body: $e^{2z}=e^ze^z$. The coefficient of $\frac{z^n}{n!}$ on the left is $2^n$. By the product formula applied with $a_m=b_m=1$, it is $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\cdot1\cdot1$ on the right. Hence $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk=2^n$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-17.title: Double counting
bmt-2021-power-17.body: Count the subsets of an $n$-element set $X$. Each element is either in or out of the subset, so there are $2^n$ subsets. Alternatively, for each $k$ there are $\binom nk$ subsets of size $k$, so there are $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk$ subsets in total. Hence the two counts agree. ∎

bmt-2021-power-18.title: Pick two involutions
bmt-2021-power-18.body:
$(2143)'$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow2$ and $3\leftrightarrow4$, so applying it twice gives the identity; $(4321)'$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow4$ and $2\leftrightarrow3$, also an involution. Any other involutions of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ are fine too.

**Answer: e.g. $(2143)'$ and $(4321)'$**

bmt-2021-power-19.title: Relabeling
bmt-2021-power-19.body:
$T[V_1]$ consists of the trees with $5$ vertices labeled by $1,\dots,5$ and $T[V_2]$ of the trees with $5$ vertices labeled by $a,\dots,e$. Renaming $1,2,3,4,5$ as $a,b,c,d,e$ turns one set into the other, so the only difference is the names of the labels.

**Answer: only the labels differ**

bmt-2021-power-20.title: Interpretation and count
bmt-2021-power-20.body:
$\mathrm{Par}[U]$ is the set of all ways to split $U$ into non-empty disjoint subsets (blocks). An example is $\{1,2\}\cup\{3\}\cup\{4\}$. The number of set partitions of a $4$-element set is the Bell number $\mathrm{Par}(4)=15$ (Question 1.13).

**Answer: 15**

bmt-2021-power-21a.title: Split off the fixed points
bmt-2021-power-21a.body: Given a permutation $\sigma$ of $U$, let $U_1$ be its set of fixed points and $U_2=U\setminus U_1$. Then $\sigma$ restricted to $U_2$ is a permutation with no fixed point, i.e. a derangement of $U_2$. Conversely, a set $U_1$ (a $\mathrm{Set}$-structure on $U_1$) together with a derangement of the complement $U_2$ determines a permutation of $U$ fixing exactly $U_1$. This bijection never refers to what the elements of $U$ are, so $\mathrm{Per}=\mathrm{Set}\cdot\mathrm{Der}$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-21b.title: Inside and outside
bmt-2021-power-21b.body: A subset $A\subseteq U$ corresponds to the ordered pair (the set $A$, the set $U\setminus A$), i.e. to a $\mathrm{Set}$-structure on $A$ and a $\mathrm{Set}$-structure on $U\setminus A$ for a partition of $U$ into two parts. Conversely such a pair determines the subset $A$. The bijection does not depend on the elements of $U$, so $P=\mathrm{Set}\cdot\mathrm{Set}$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-22a.title: Blocks are non-empty sets
bmt-2021-power-22a.body: A set partition of $U$ is a set of non-empty subsets (blocks) whose disjoint union is $U$. Each block is a $\mathrm{Set}^+$-structure on itself, and the blocks form a partition of $U$, so a partition is exactly a $\mathrm{Set}\circ\mathrm{Set}^+$-structure. The correspondence does not depend on the labels, so $\mathrm{Par}=\mathrm{Set}\circ\mathrm{Set}^+$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-22b.title: Cycle decomposition
bmt-2021-power-22b.body: By Question 1.8, a permutation $\sigma$ of $U$ decomposes into disjoint cycles, whose supports partition $U$; on each support $\sigma$ is a cyclic permutation, i.e. a $\mathrm{Cyc}$-structure. The decomposition is unique (the cycle through $x$ is determined by $\sigma$), and conversely any set of cyclic permutations on the blocks of a partition of $U$ defines a permutation of $U$. The correspondence does not depend on the labels, so $\mathrm{Per}=\mathrm{Set}\circ\mathrm{Cyc}$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-23a.title: Disjoint union
bmt-2021-power-23a.body: By definition $(F+G)[U]$ is the disjoint union of $F[U]$ and $G[U]$ (if the sets overlap, tag the elements with which species they come from). So $h_n=|(F+G)[n]|=f_n+g_n$, and $H(z)=\sum(f_n+g_n)\frac{z^n}{n!}=F(z)+G(z)$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-23b.title: Count product structures
bmt-2021-power-23b.body: A $(F\cdot G)$-structure on $[n]$ is a choice of a set $U_1\subseteq[n]$, with $U_2=[n]\setminus U_1$, together with an $F$-structure on $U_1$ and a $G$-structure on $U_2$. For $|U_1|=k$ there are $\binom nk$ choices of $U_1$, and for each $f_kg_{n-k}$ pairs of structures (the number of $F$-structures on a $k$-set is $f_k$, since relabeling gives a bijection with $F[\{1..k\}]$). Hence $q_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkf_kg_{n-k}$. By Question 2.2 this says exactly that $Q(z)=F(z)G(z)$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-24.title: Involutions are sets of 1-cycles and 2-cycles
bmt-2021-power-24.body:
If $\sigma$ is an involution and $(c_1\,c_2\,\dots\,c_\ell)$ one of its cycles with $\ell\ge3$, then $\sigma^2(c_1)=c_3\ne c_1$, contradiction. So all cycles have length $1$ or $2$; conversely any permutation with only such cycles satisfies $\sigma^2=e$. Hence $I=\mathrm{Set}\circ(\mathrm{Cyc}_1+\mathrm{Cyc}_2)$.

**The EGF of $\mathrm{Cyc}_j$ (cycles of length exactly $j$) is $\frac{z^j}{j}$:** a cycle on $j$ labeled elements can be written in $j!$ orderings, and each cycle arises from $j$ of them (rotations), so there are $(j-1)!$ cycles on $j$ points and none on other numbers of points; thus the EGF is $(j-1)!\frac{z^j}{j!}=\frac{z^j}{j}$.

By Theorem 3 and Question 4.1(a), $I(z)=\exp\left(\frac z1+\frac{z^2}2\right)=e^z\cdot e^{z^2/2}$.

Now $e^{z^2/2}=T(z)$ is the EGF of the number $t_\ell$ of pairings (Question 2.1(b)), and $e^z$ has all coefficients $1$. By Question 2.2, $I_n=\sum_{\ell=0}^n\binom n\ell t_\ell$, and since $t_\ell=0$ for odd $\ell$ and $t_{2k}=\frac{(2k)!}{2^kk!}$, we get $I_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom n{2k}\frac{(2k)!}{k!\,2^k}$. (Check: $I_4=1+6\cdot1+1\cdot3=10$.) ∎

bmt-2021-power-25.title: Cycle lengths divide m
bmt-2021-power-25.body:
**Lemma.** $\sigma^m=e$ iff every cycle of $\sigma$ has length dividing $m$. If a cycle of $\sigma$ has length $\ell$ and contains $a$, then $\sigma^m(a)$ is the element $m$ steps ahead of $a$ along the cycle, which equals $a$ iff $\ell\mid m$. So $\sigma^m=e$ forces $\ell\mid m$ for all cycles. Conversely if every cycle length $\ell_i$ divides $m$, each cycle $\tau_i$ satisfies $\tau_i^{\ell_i}=e$ hence $\tau_i^m=e$, and since the cycles act on disjoint sets, $\sigma^m=\prod\tau_i^m=e$.

Hence $U_m=\mathrm{Set}\circ\sum_{d\mid m}\mathrm{Cyc}_d$. **The EGF of $\mathrm{Cyc}_j$ (cycles of length exactly $j$) is $\frac{z^j}{j}$:** a cycle on $j$ labeled elements can be written in $j!$ orderings, and each cycle arises from $j$ of them (rotations), so there are $(j-1)!$ cycles on $j$ points and none on other numbers of points; thus the EGF is $(j-1)!\frac{z^j}{j!}=\frac{z^j}{j}$. By Theorem 3 and Question 4.1(a), $U_m(z)=\exp\left(\sum_{d\mid m}\frac{z^d}{d}\right)$. ∎

bmt-2021-power-26.title: EGF and telescoping

bmt-2021-power-27.title: EGF of permutations with all cycles long
bmt-2021-power-27.body:
A permutation has shortest cycle longer than $k$ iff all its cycles have length $>k$, so $\mathrm{Per}_{>k}=\mathrm{Set}\circ\mathrm{Cyc}_{>k}$. Since $\mathrm{Cyc}=\mathrm{Cyc}_{>k}+\mathrm{Cyc}_1+\cdots+\mathrm{Cyc}_k$ and $\mathrm{Cyc}_j(z)=\frac{z^j}j$, $\mathrm{Cyc}(z)=\ln\frac1{1-z}$, we get
$$\mathrm{Cyc}_{>k}(z)=\ln\frac1{1-z}-\left(z+\frac{z^2}2+\cdots+\frac{z^k}k\right),\qquad \hat P_{>k}(z)=\frac{\exp\left(-\left(z+\frac{z^2}2+\cdots+\frac{z^k}k\right)\right)}{1-z}.$$
Exactly as in Question 4.4 (telescoping), the probability $\hat P_{>k}(n)/n!$ equals the $n$-th partial sum of $(1-z)\hat P_{>k}(z)$ at $z=1$, so its limit is
$$\left.\exp\left(-\left(z+\tfrac{z^2}2+\cdots+\tfrac{z^k}k\right)\right)\right|_{z=1}=e^{-(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1k)}\approx e^{-\ln k-\gamma}=\frac1{e^{\gamma}k}.$$ ∎
